summary: Pupils (ages 11–14) derive the interior-angle sum of a polygon by splitting it into n−2 triangles from one vertex ((n−2)×180°), feel the exterior-angle total of 360° by walking the perimeter, and carefully separate the two 'totals' they confuse: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex, versus all exterior angles = 360° for the WHOLE polygon. Dividing by n (sum÷n for each interior, 360÷n for each exterior) gives each angle ONLY when all the angles are equal. This is true of every regular polygon (the KS3 focus), and also of equal-angled shapes such as a non-square rectangle. The angle sum depends on the number of sides, not the polygon's size. The strongest route is proposed to be a construction the child performs (triangulate, walk the perimeter, toggle regular/irregular); fixed diagrams and scored questions are useful support with stated limits.
misconceptions: Thinking a triangle's angles sum to 360°
Dividing 360° (or the interior sum) by n for an IRREGULAR polygon, or assuming all its angles are equal
Believing a bigger polygon has a bigger angle sum (angle scales with size)
Reporting the interior-angle SUM as though it were one interior angle (forgetting to divide by n)

activities.title: Triangulate to build the angle sum
steps: Start with a polygon whose number of sides you can change. Before calculating, predict: what do all its interior angles add to?
Split the polygon into triangles by drawing diagonals from one corner. Count the triangles: a pentagon gives 3, a hexagon gives 4.
Record the running total as (number of triangles)×180°: pentagon 3×180 = 540°, hexagon 4×180 = 720°.
State the general pattern in your own words: splitting from one corner, a convex n-sided polygon always makes n−2 triangles, so the interior sum is (n−2)×180°.
Add two more sides and confirm the sum GROWS with the number of sides — not with the polygon's size.
activities.insight: The interior-angle sum (n−2)×180° is a consequence of how many triangles the polygon decomposes into, and it depends on the number of sides, not the size.

activities.title: Walk the perimeter: exterior angles total 360°
steps: Imagine (or move a marker) walking around the outside of the polygon, turning at each corner to follow the next side.
Add up all the turns you make to get back to your starting direction.
Repeat for convex polygons with different numbers of sides and confirm the turns always total exactly 360°, however many sides there are.
At a single chosen corner, mark the interior angle and the exterior angle sitting together on a straight line, and check they sum to 180°.
Say aloud the difference between the two totals: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex; ALL exterior angles together = 360° for the whole polygon.
activities.insight: Walking the perimeter of a convex polygon means turning through one full 360° in total, so the exterior angles sum to 360°, regardless of the number of sides — a separate fact from the 180° interior/exterior pair at a single vertex.

activities.title: Regular or irregular: when may you divide by n?
steps: Take a regular pentagon: find the interior sum by triangulation (3×180 = 540°), then find EACH interior angle by dividing by n (540÷5 = 108°).
Find each exterior angle two ways and check they agree: 180 − 108 = 72° and 360÷5 = 72°.

Compare two hexagons that have the SAME interior sum of 720°: a regular hexagon, where ÷6 gives each angle = 720÷6 = 120°, and an irregular hexagon, where the angles are visibly unequal so no single quotient describes them all.

For the irregular hexagon, divide 720 by 6 to get 120°, then compare with the figure: its angles are not all equal, so 120° cannot be each angle — ÷n does not give each angle of a polygon whose angles are unequal (even if one angle happened to equal the quotient).
Instead, find ONE missing angle of the irregular hexagon by subtracting the five known angles from 720°.

Write the rule: you may divide the sum by n to get each angle ONLY when every angle is equal, as in every regular polygon (a rectangle shows that equal angles are enough, even if the sides differ); the sum itself is the same for any hexagon.
activities.insight: Dividing the interior sum by n (or using 360÷n for exterior) gives each angle ONLY when all the angles are equal, as in a regular polygon. Two polygons with the same number of sides share the same interior sum, but for one with unequal angles a missing angle is found by subtracting the known angles rather than by dividing.

activities.title: Triangle angle sum: 180°, not 360°
steps: Find the third angle of a triangle whose other two angles are 70° and 60° by subtracting from 180°: 180 − 70 − 60 = 50°.
Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange them against a straight edge; observe they fit along a straight line (180°).
Contrast this straight-line 180° with a full turn of 360° so the two 'wholes' are kept apart.
Explain why you subtracted from 180° and not 360°.
activities.insight: A triangle's interior angles sum to 180° (a straight line), which is a different whole from the 360° of a full turn; a missing angle is found by subtracting the known angles from 180°.

activities.title: Check and consolidate with mixed questions
steps: Give the interior-angle sum of a named polygon (e.g. octagon → (8−2)×180 = 1080°).
For a regular polygon, give BOTH an interior angle and its matching exterior angle, and state how they relate (sum to 180° at a vertex).
Answer a question that contrasts interior versus exterior angles, and identify why a tempting wrong option (dividing the sum by n for an irregular polygon whose angles are unequal) is invalid.
Order several polygons by their interior-angle sum and explain what the ordering depends on (number of sides).
activities.insight: Named-polygon sums, interior/exterior relationships and the regular-only condition can be recalled and applied fluently and distinguished from common distractors.

checkQuestion: Give the child three figures and a pencil: (a) a triangle with two angles marked 70° and 60°; (b) an IRREGULAR hexagon; (c) a regular pentagon. Set them to: (a) find the third angle; (b) find the sum of the interior angles of the hexagon, showing how — invite them to split it up — then find one missing angle given the other five; (c) find EACH interior angle and EACH exterior angle of the regular pentagon. Watch whether they subtract from 180 (not 360) for the triangle, whether they split the hexagon into triangles to get (n−2)×180, whether they divide by n only because the pentagon is regular, and whether they keep interior and exterior angles distinct.
checkAnswer: (a) 180 − 70 − 60 = 50°. (b) The hexagon splits into 4 triangles from one vertex, so the interior sum is 4×180 = 720°; a missing angle is 720 minus the other five. (c) Regular pentagon interior sum = 3×180 = 540°, so each interior angle = 540÷5 = 108°; each exterior angle = 180 − 108 = 72° (equivalently 360÷5 = 72°). The child derives the sum by triangulation and divides by n only because the pentagon is stated to be regular.
